introduction-the-aws-native-orchestrator.core: ECS is AWS's own container orchestrator: a free, fully managed control plane deeply integrated with IAM, ALB, CloudWatch, Cloud Map and Service Connect. You define tasks and services; ECS schedules them onto EC2 or Fargate capacity. It's simpler than Kubernetes, with fewer concepts and less to operate.

first_principles.problem: A small team wants to run containers on AWS without Kubernetes complexity.
truths: Orchestration needs scheduling, health and scaling.
Fewer abstractions mean less to learn.

analogy.title: An appliance with sensible defaults versus a modular hi-fi kit
analogy.story: It just works for most needs, with fewer knobs.
analogy.breaks: Appliances can't be extended much; ECS lacks Kubernetes' ecosystem of operators and CRDs.

example.title: Deploy a web service
flow: Register task definition (image, CPU, memory, port)
Create service with desired count 3 behind ALB

check.q: What does the ECS control plane cost?
check.a: Nothing; you pay only for the compute (EC2 or Fargate) and other resources.

task-definitions-the-blueprint.core: A task definition is a versioned JSON blueprint: container images, CPU/memory, port mappings, environment and secrets (from Secrets Manager/SSM), log configuration, health checks, volumes, network mode (awsvpc), and two IAM roles: the task execution role (pull images, write logs, fetch secrets) and the task role (the app's AWS permissions).

first_principles.problem: Secrets are baked into images and every container shares broad permissions.
truths: Configuration should be declarative and versioned.
Platform actions and app actions need different permissions.
Secrets must not live in images.

analogy.title: A recipe card for a dish
analogy.story: Ingredients, quantities, cooking method and which kitchen tools it may use.
analogy.breaks: Recipe cards get edited in place; task definitions are immutable revisions.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Secrets injected at runtime; least-privilege app role.

check.q: What's the difference between the task execution role and the task role?
check.a: The execution role lets ECS pull images, push logs and fetch secrets; the task role grants the application's own AWS permissions.

services-the-fleet-manager.core: An ECS service keeps a desired number of tasks running, replaces unhealthy ones, registers them with load balancer target groups, autoscales on metrics, and deploys new revisions using rolling updates (with the deployment circuit breaker for automatic rollback) or blue/green via CodeDeploy.

first_principles.problem: A bad deploy keeps replacing healthy tasks with crashing ones until the service is down.
derivation: Attach **ALB target groups** and health checks.

analogy.title: A shift supervisor keeping enough staff on the floor
analogy.story: Replaces anyone who leaves, staggers shift changes and calls more people in when it's busy.
analogy.breaks: Supervisors use judgement; services follow configured thresholds exactly.

check.q: What does the ECS deployment circuit breaker do?
check.a: Detects a deployment that can't reach steady state and, if enabled, rolls back to the last working revision.

capacity-providers-the-bridge-to-infrast.core: Capacity providers connect services to infrastructure: FARGATE, FARGATE_SPOT, or EC2 Auto Scaling groups with managed scaling (ECS scales the ASG to fit tasks) and managed termination protection. Capacity provider strategies split tasks by base and weight, e.g. a base on Fargate and the rest on Fargate Spot.

first_principles.problem: An EC2-backed cluster runs out of capacity and tasks sit in PROVISIONING.
truths: Cluster capacity must track task demand.
derivation: Use **ASG capacity providers with managed scaling** for EC2.

analogy.title: Staffing agencies supplying workers
analogy.story: You tell the supervisor how many workers you want from each agency.
analogy.breaks: Agencies send people instantly; EC2 capacity takes minutes to launch.

check.q: What does managed scaling on an ASG capacity provider do?
check.a: ECS adjusts the ASG's desired capacity to fit the tasks that need placing, at the configured target capacity.

ecs-vs-eks-the-trade-offs.core: ECS is simpler, AWS-native and free at the control-plane level, which is great for teams standardised on AWS that want low operational overhead. EKS offers the Kubernetes ecosystem, portability and extensibility (CRDs, operators, Helm) at the cost of more complexity and a per-cluster fee. Choose by team skills, ecosystem needs and multi-cloud requirements.

first_principles.problem: A startup adopts Kubernetes for prestige and spends a quarter on platform work instead of product.
truths: Portability matters only if you'll use it.
derivation: **ECS** for AWS-only, small teams, simple services.
**EKS** for Kubernetes skills, ecosystem tools, portability.

analogy.title: An automatic car versus a manual sports car
analogy.story: The automatic is easy and reliable; the manual gives control and fun but needs skill.
analogy.breaks: Cars don't come with app stores; Kubernetes' ecosystem is a major part of its value.

example.title: Two organisations
flow: 10-engineer SaaS, AWS only → ECS on Fargate
Platform team, 300 engineers, operators and GitOps → EKS

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Fit the tool to the team.

check.q: When is EKS the better choice than ECS?
check.a: When you need the Kubernetes ecosystem (operators, Helm, CRDs), existing Kubernetes skills or portability across clouds.
